To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the information content of China's official GDP data is low, but (ii) a simple index based on four non GDP variables is highly correlated with Chinese activity in both sample and out of sample periods.
the information content in Chinese GDP has improved substantially since 2008 and that a set of four non GDP indicators, without GDP, provides a more reliable measure of Chinese economic activity.
the information content and reliability of China's GDP and economic activity data have improved substantially since 2008.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two main issues: (i) the quality of Chinese data and (ii) the reliability of the most widely used Chinese output measure.

two issues: (i) the extent to which China's official statistics are credible and (ii) whether there is an alternative set of data sources that can be used to construct a more reliable measure of Chinese economic activity.
the question: how reliable are China's official economic data? In particular, we focus on the accuracy of China's official GDP figures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Chinese data are not reliable, and that the best way to proceed is to ignore GDP and use alternative indicators of economic activity.
the Chinese GDP series is unreliable as an indicator of economic activity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
China's official GDP figures are a useful indicator of activity, but that they are not as reliable as the alternative indicators that are available.
the information content in Chinese GDP is low in the pre 2008 period, but that the information content improves markedly after 2010.
China has made significant strides in the quality of its economic statistics since 2008, but the quality of the statistics still lags that of the major advanced economies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the information content in Chinese economic data is improving.

the Chinese economy is much larger than the GDP figures suggest, with the gap growing over time, and that the best measures of economic activity do not include GDP.
